purpose: Improve the actual existing first-school-mock short-recall marker for 14 previously sampled uncalibrated Physics Mechanics and Measurements cards, without adding duplicates.
safeguards: Original IDs, original question fronts, original model answers and student progress remain unchanged.
Only AS Physics cards with mock=true and matching exact original wording are patched; do not alter full-only or modified cards.
Keep existing accepted and rejected variants when present, and test every original model answer.
No written multi-mark exam questions hidden inside flashcards, no XP/cloud sync changes.
No conclusion that every AQA Physics assessment objective or unseen answer is covered.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalBack: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.
accept: Accuracy means close to the true value; precision means repeated values are close together.
reject: Accuracy is when repeated measurements agree, even if they are far from the true value.
Precision means closeness to the true value and accuracy means repeatability.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How is a percentage gradient uncertainty estimated from graph lines?
accept: Percentage gradient uncertainty is the difference between best and worst acceptable gradients divided by the best gradient magnitude, times 100.
reject: Divide the best gradient by the difference between the best and worst slopes.
Use the x intercept as the denominator instead of the best-fit gradient.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do you combine uncertainties when adding or subtracting measurements?
accept: For addition or subtraction of measured quantities, sum their absolute uncertainties.
reject: When subtracting readings, subtract their absolute uncertainties too.
Add their percentage uncertainties when adding lengths, rather than absolute uncertainties.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why does percentage uncertainty in wire diameter approximately double for cross-sectional area?
rows.originalBack: Area A = πd²/4, so percentage uncertainty in A ≈ 2 × percentage uncertainty in d.
accept: Since wire area is proportional to diameter squared, its percentage uncertainty is approximately double the diameter's.
reject: Cross-sectional area has half the percentage uncertainty of diameter.
Uncertainty in diameter never affects uncertainty in wire cross-sectional area.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why does increasing the measured interval often reduce percentage uncertainty?
rows.originalBack: The absolute uncertainty is similar but becomes a smaller fraction of a larger measured value.
accept: A similar absolute reading uncertainty is a smaller fraction of a larger measured time or distance.
reject: The measuring instrument becomes more precise simply because a larger interval is measured.
With constant absolute uncertainty, the percentage uncertainty increases when the measured interval increases.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why can a couple turn an object without a resultant force?
rows.originalBack: Its two equal, opposite, parallel forces cancel as forces, but act along separate lines to cause turning.
accept: The two equal opposite parallel forces have zero resultant, but separate lines of action create a turning effect.
reject: The two forces act on the same line and so make a nonzero couple.
A couple needs forces of different magnitudes to provide a resultant force.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: When resolving a vector, what decides whether to use sin or cos?
rows.originalBack: Look at the marked angle: adjacent side uses cos θ; opposite side uses sin θ. Never rely on horizontal or vertical.
accept: Use cosine for the component adjacent to the given angle and sine for the opposite component.
reject: The horizontal component always uses sine, regardless of where the angle is measured.
The adjacent component uses sine and the opposite component uses cosine.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: On a slope, which way do weight and its two components act?
rows.originalBack: Weight mg acts vertically down; mg sin θ acts down the slope; mg cos θ acts into the slope.
accept: Weight acts vertically down; mg sin theta points downhill along the slope and mg cos theta pushes into the slope.
reject: Weight acts at right angles to the slope rather than vertically downwards.
mg cos theta acts downhill and mg sin theta acts into the slope.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Ignoring air resistance, which force acts on a projectile after release?
rows.originalBack: Only weight (gravity) acts, vertically downwards; no forward driving force is needed.
accept: Once released and neglecting drag, a projectile only experiences gravity acting downwards.
reject: A forward driving force continues acting for the whole flight after release.
At the top of the flight, no force acts on the projectile.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What stays constant horizontally in ideal projectile motion?
accept: The horizontal component of velocity remains constant because horizontal acceleration is zero.
reject: Gravity acts horizontally, reducing the projectile's horizontal velocity.
Horizontal acceleration is g and the vertical acceleration is zero.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the vertical acceleration during ideal projectile motion?
accept: The projectile's vertical acceleration is constant g acting downwards.
reject: Vertical acceleration becomes zero at the highest point.
Vertical acceleration is g upwards during the ascent and g downwards during descent.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the principle of moments in equilibrium?
rows.originalBack: Total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about the same point.
accept: For rotational equilibrium, the total clockwise moments equal the total anticlockwise moments about one point.
reject: In equilibrium, clockwise moments must be larger than anticlockwise moments.
Only one force's moment is relevant when deciding if an object is balanced.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: In an inelastic collision of an isolated system, which quantities are conserved?
rows.originalBack: Total momentum is conserved; total kinetic energy need not be conserved.
accept: An isolated inelastic collision conserves total momentum; total kinetic energy can decrease.
reject: Both momentum and kinetic energy must always be conserved in any inelastic collision.
Total momentum is lost in every inelastic collision even when no external force acts.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What condition allows use of conservation of momentum?
rows.originalBack: No external resultant force acts on the system.
accept: The resultant external force on the system must be zero or negligible.
reject: Any external resultant force is allowed provided the collision happens quickly.
Momentum is conserved only when kinetic energy is also conserved.
